description: We are NEU Marswalk, a team building Marswalk: an EVA planner and helmet HUD that lets Mars astronauts plan and rehearse safe walks on real NASA terrain (HiRISE, THEMIS, CRISM). We love space, maps, 3D graphics and data. Our skills: web development (JavaScript, Three.js), Python data processing, and GIS. We’d welcome teammates with skills in UI/UX design, video editing, planetary science, or public speaking. Join us to explore Mars one step at a time!
summary: Marswalk is an EVA planner and helmet HUD for a Mars astronaut who works with a rover partner. The astronaut picks a site on a 3D Mars globe, reads its science goal, and chooses stops on real 1 m HiRISE terrain. A route planner avoids steep, rough and soft-sand ground and gives a GO / CAUTION / NO-GO verdict with clear reasons: oxygen and battery margin, the walk-back limit, radio line of sight, sand-trap risk, radiation and nightfall. The astronaut then rehearses the walk in first person, with the real Mars sun and clock, physical hazards, real Curiosity and Perseverance photos at each stop, and a scored debrief. The map layers combine data from five NASA missions: HiRISE terrain and images, THEMIS thermal data, CRISM minerals, MOLA/TES globe maps, rover traverses, plus live Curiosity weather and NASA DONKI space weather. Five sites are ready, including the Gale boxwork named in the challenge, and one script builds a new site from any HiRISE terrain model. NASA's first priority is crew safety. Marswalk lets a crew test every walk before the hatch opens, in a web browser, with nothing to install.
details:
What it does Marswalk answers the questions a crew asks before an EVA: Can I get there and back safely, on foot or by rover? How much oxygen, battery and radiation dose will it cost? Where could I get stuck, lose contact, or be caught by a solar storm? What will each stop look like, and what science is there?

It has three screens, matching the displays named in the challenge:

  1. Habitat display: a 3D Mars globe with real sub-solar lighting. Pick one of five sites (Jezero, Jezero delta front, Gale, Gale boxwork, Mawrth Vallis). Each site states its science goal.
  2. Planning tablet: real 1 m terrain in 3D with 8 data layers (hazards, safety, science). Choose stops, ride or walk, payload and start time. The planner returns a route and a GO / CAUTION / NO-GO verdict, with a reason for every risk and an elevation profile.
  3. Helmet HUD: walk the planned route in first person. Day and night follow Mars time. Rocks and the habitat are solid, sand can trap the rover, oxygen and battery run down, and a solar storm drill sends you to the nearest shelter. At each stop a science card shows the mineral, thermal and elevation data and a real rover photo taken there. The rehearsal ends with a planned-versus-actual debrief. The plan can be shared as a link or printed as an EVA cuff card.

How it works A Python pipeline crops a 2.56 km window from a HiRISE terrain model and image, computes slope and 1 m roughness, and adds THEMIS night-time infrared (loose sand stays cold at night), CRISM mineral maps, and rover photos matched to where they were taken. In the browser, an A* search on a 10 m grid finds the route. The cost includes slope, roughness, soft sand and, during a solar storm, terrain shelter. A Dijkstra field from the habitat enforces the Apollo-style walk-back rule: at every point, the astronaut must be able to walk home on the remaining oxygen if the rover fails. Radio coverage is a line-of-sight trace from a 6 m mast. Mars time and sun position use NASA's Mars24 algorithm.

Benefits and impact

  • Safety first: every risk has a number and a reason, so the crew and mission control can agree on GO or NO-GO.
  • Rehearsal: the crew sees the hazards and the destination before leaving the habitat, which lowers surprise and workload outside.
  • Science return: stops are chosen by science value, and the crew knows what to look for at each one.
  • Open and portable: it runs in any web browser, uses only public NASA data, and any of the more than 1,000 HiRISE terrain models can become a new site with one script. Students and the public can also use it to explore real Mars terrain.

Tools JavaScript, HTML and CSS; Three.js for 3D. Python 3 with rasterio (GDAL), NumPy and Pillow for the data pipeline. The site is static, with no server code. Git and GitHub for version control. We used Claude (Anthropic), to help write code and documents.

What is creative

  • It starts from a science goal, then checks safety, then lets the astronaut rehearse. Most Mars maps only show data.
  • It turns raw data into decisions: night-time infrared plus image brightness becomes a soft-sand warning, and terrain becomes a walk-back limit and radio coverage.
  • Real rover photos appear exactly where they were taken, so the astronaut sees the real place before arriving.
  • It mixes real data with live conditions: today's Curiosity weather report and recent solar particle events from NASA DONKI.

What we considered

  • Honesty about data: every layer is marked REAL DATA or MODEL. Terrain, images, minerals and photos are real. Weather curves, walking speed and oxygen use are estimates fitted to published ranges.
  • Astronaut limits: suit mobility, carried equipment, oxygen, battery, cold nights, radiation, and the rover as a partner that can fail.
  • Performance: only the needed parts of large NASA files are downloaded, and far-away rocks are not drawn, so it runs on a laptop.
  • Limits: sites are separate 2.56 km tiles, rock positions are generated from real roughness, and two-astronaut EVAs are not modelled yet.

Mars Odyssey THEMIS night IR controlled mosaics (USGS Astrogeology)
MRO CRISM MTRDR products (PDS Geosciences Node)
Mars Orbital Data Explorer (ODE), used to find CRISM products
NASA DONKI space weather, solar energetic particle events (via api.nasa.gov)
MGS MOLA / THEMIS blend and MGS TES albedo global mosaics (USGS Astrogeology, NASA PDS)
Mars 2020 MEDA and MSL REMS climate data (PDS Atmospheres Node)
Mars Science Laboratory mission (RAD radiation results)
